metadata.title: Gary Marcus Warns OpenAI Could Become ‘WeWork Of AI’ — And Nvidia May Pay The Price

content.text:

Marcus added that the bigger concern, however, is what happens if OpenAI cannot sustain its current valuation and is forced to seek an alternative.
NYU Professor Emeritus Gary Marcus believes that OpenAI's ambitions and delayed IPO plans are raising uncomfortable questions about the sustainability of the artificial intelligence boom.
During an interview with CNBC, Marcus warned that growing skepticism around generative AI, rising financing costs and questions about whether companies can monetize their investments could expose vulnerabilities across the AI ecosystem.
He added that the company could become a cautionary tale for the industry, with potentially wider consequences for Nvidia Corp. (NVDA).
OpenAI Could Become The 'WeWork of AI,' Marcus Warns
Marcus questioned whether OpenAI's business trajectory can live up to the expectations surrounding it. Drawing a comparison with WeWork, the once high-flying office-sharing company that never went public, he pointed to OpenAI's repeatedly delayed IPO plans as a potential warning sign.
"OpenAI, for example, I've long talked about as possibly being the WeWork of AI," Marcus said.
He noted that WeWork never completed its IPO, while OpenAI continues to push its own listing plans back. Marcus added that the bigger concern, however, is what happens if OpenAI cannot sustain its current valuation and is forced to seek an alternative.
"What if OpenAI is forced to sell at a discount to something like Microsoft?" Marcus asked. He then raised the potential consequences for Nvidia, whose chips have powered much of the industry's AI infrastructure spending.
"What would be the effect on Nvidia of that if they're kind of poster child had to take a big hit," he said.
Nvidia's Biggest AI Risk May Be Whether Customers Can Make Money
Marcus believes Nvidia's strong technology and execution do not necessarily guarantee that demand for its chips will continue growing indefinitely.
"I think Nvidia is very well run. The chips are great, but there's a question about whether there's infinite demand and whether the companies buying it can make a profit from it," he said.
He also warned that the AI infrastructure boom could face a financing crunch, particularly among neocloud companies that depend heavily on external funding to expand their computing capacity.
